title: Devadatta's plots
hookLine: the boulder rolled down, the elephant sent, the split in the community (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)

cards: A slope below Vulture's Peak, outside Rajagaha. The Buddha is walking in the shade of the hill. Up on the ridge, a man shoves a large rock over the edge.
The Vinaya says the rock was stopped before it reached him, but a splinter broke off, struck the Buddha's foot, and drew blood. The man on the ridge is Devadatta.
The Cullavagga tells his story as a chain: hired men on a road, a falling rock, an elephant set loose, and last, the one the text slows down for.

teach.h: HIRED MEN WHO SAT DOWN TO LISTEN.
teach.b: First, the hired men. In the Vinaya's telling, Devadatta sends men to kill the Buddha on a road. One by one they arrive, lose their nerve, sit down, and hear him teach.
Second, the rock, which Devadatta tries himself. Afterward, the Vinaya has the Buddha tell his monks that no one can take a Tathagata's life by violence. Third, the elephant.
Devadatta gets the keepers to turn Nalagiri, a fierce elephant, loose on the road where the Buddha walks for alms. People scatter.
The Buddha meets him with loving-kindness, metta, and the text says the elephant lowers his trunk, takes dust from the Buddha's feet, scatters it on his own head, and backs away.
Fourth, the split, and here the story changes key. Devadatta goes after the community.
He proposes five strict rules: live in the forest, eat only alms food, wear only rag robes, sleep under trees, eat no fish or meat. They sound devout.

The Buddha answers that any monk who wishes may keep them, but he won't make them binding on all. Devadatta says this proves the Buddha has gone soft, gathers newly ordained monks, and leads them away to Gayasisa.
The Buddha had already warned him that splitting the sangha is a grave thing, and tradition says it is one of the deeds that bring the heaviest results.
But the chapter doesn't end with the split. Sariputta and Moggallana walk to Gayasisa, teach the young monks, and bring them home.

how: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Devadatta's plots from the Vinaya as a warning about envy and ambition, and the scene of the elephant Nalagiri calmed by loving-kindness appears in Buddhist art and in retellings of the Buddha's life.

o: attacks on the Buddha, then a split in the sangha
strict rules the Buddha made binding on everyone
a plot of land Devadatta gave to the monks

s: the elephant charged and the Buddha ran
he met Nalagiri with loving-kindness, and the elephant lowered his trunk and backed away.
the Buddha made Devadatta's five rules binding on every monk
he said any monk who wished could keep them, but he wouldn't require them.
Sariputta and Moggallana brought the young monks back
they walked to Gayasisa, taught the monks Devadatta had led away, and brought them home.

games.q: Devadatta asks the Buddha to make five strict rules binding on every monk: forest, alms food only, rag robes, sleeping under trees, no fish or meat. what does the Buddha say?
o: let anyone who wishes keep them, but require none.
games.why: he leaves them open to anyone who wishes and refuses to require them. Devadatta uses the refusal to split the community.

practice: Let one small split come to mind: two friends who stopped talking, a family thread gone quiet, a coworker you've been routing around.
See where you stand in it, and look for one small step back across the line, a question or a plain hello. You don't have to take it yet; just find it, and hold it while the breath moves.

wordCard.voice: Devadatta's plots. Hired men, a rock, a fierce elephant, and finally a split in the sangha, the one the Buddha called grave. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali saṅghabheda: a split in the sangha, the community of monks and nuns.

carryVoice: Your line: the split. A rock wounds a foot; a split wounds the thing that carries the teaching forward. See you tomorrow.
